sentences.text: Berberosaurus was a moderate-sized bipedal carnivore with a femur measuring exactly 50.5 centimeters in length.
Based on this bone, researchers estimate the total length of the animal was approximately five meters.
Its neck vertebrae were highly pneumatic, featuring short centra and holes in the neural arch.
This specific structure is distinct from that seen in Elaphrosaurus and Ceratosaurus.
Distinctive features include an arched sacral series and a grooved proximal metacarpal.
The femoral trochanter reaches the midpoint of the femoral head.
Additionally, the distal tibia is subtriangular, and an oblique ridge covers the fibula's medial sulcus.
The genus was named after the Berbers of Morocco and found in the Central High Atlas.
Remains were discovered during expeditions to the High Atlas starting in the early 2000s over a period of more than six years.
The type specimen is a partial postcranial skeleton of a subadult individual housed in the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle de Marrakech.
Fossils were found in bone beds within mudflow deposits alongside Tazoudasaurus and an indeterminate large theropod.
New material including an axis, postorbital, cranium, and teeth has been recovered from the same area and is currently under study.
Initial remains were discovered in expeditions to the Toundoute Atlas Mountains near Ouarzazate, Morocco, in the year 2000.
The remains were found in a bone bed that was once a swamp.
Ronan Allain and colleagues described the dinosaur.
Remains of Berberosaurus were found near those of the early sauropod Tazoudasaurus and another small theropod.
It is considered the most basal member of Abelisauroidea, more evolved than Elaphrosaurus, Ceratosauridae, and Spinostropheus, but less evolved than Xenotarsosaurus and Abelisaurus.
The parent group of Berberosaurus is Ceratosauridae.
Berberosaurus belongs to the family Ceratosauridae.
The type species of the genus Berberosaurus is Berberosaurus liassicus.
Carrano and Sampson in 2008 classified it as a basal ceratosaur outside Neoceratosauria.
This classification differed from the abelisauroid classification proposed by others.
Xu et al. in 2009 recovered it as a dilophosaurid in an unresolved polytomy with Dilophosaurus wetherilli, Dilophosaurus sinensis, Dracovenator, and Cryolophosaurus.
Ezcurra, Agnolin, and Novas in 2010 placed Berberosaurus in an unresolved polytomy with Ceratosaurus and Abelisauroidea.
Conversely, the 2018 description of Saltriovenator places it as the sister taxon to Saltriovenator.
Berberosaurus liassicus lived during the Early Jurassic, approximately 184 to 176 million years ago, in what is now Africa.
The animal inhabited what is now Africa from the Pliensbachian to the Toarcian, between 192.9 and 174.7 million years ago.
Scientists disagree on the exact placement of Berberosaurus, with some viewing it as a basal ceratosaur, others as a dilophosaurid, and still others linking it to Ceratosaurus or Saltriovenator.
